entries.seminar_title: Watching the Oceans: Sanctions, Supply Chains, and the Global Economy
entries.speaker: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
entries.abstract: We examine the rise of dark shipping – oil tankers disabling AIS transceivers to evade detection – amid Western sanctions on Iran, Syria, North Korea, Venezuela, and Russia. Using a machine learning-based ship clustering model, we track dark-shipped crude oil trade flows worldwide and detect unauthorized ship-to-ship transfers. From 2017 to 2023, dark ships transported an estimated 7.8 million metric tons of crude oil monthly – 43% of global seaborne crude exports – with China absorbing 15%. These sanctioned flows offset recorded declines in global oil exports but create distinct economic shifts. The U.S., a net oil exporter, faces lower oil prices but benefits from cheaper Chinese imports, driving deflationary growth. The EU, a net importer, contends with rising energy costs yet gains from Chinese demand, fueling inflationary expansion. China, leveraging discounted oil, boosts industrial output, propagating global economic shocks. Our findings expose dark shipping's central role in reshaping oil markets and macroeconomic dynamics.

entries.speaker: Girija Borker
entries.abstract: We study how cuisines develop, persist, and shape economic life. Using nearly 70,000 recipes from 138 countries, we construct a novel global dataset of cuisine characteristics, ingredients, and preparation methods. We document how geography and history shape cuisines: local environmental conditions influence ingredient availability and cooking techniques, while trade and migration drive the diffusion of ingredients and culinary practices. We then examine the economic consequences of cuisine complexity, measured through cooking time, ingredient diversity, preparation intensity, and spice use. We develop a household time-allocation model in which cuisine complexity reinforces gender differences in initial returns to labor, to sustain women’s specialization in cooking. Using the flavor versatility of native spices as an instrument for cuisine complexity, together with individual-level labor market data, we find that more complex cuisines reduce women's labor force participation, particularly among married women.

entries.seminar_title: Plant-Based Policies: Subsidy Competition as a Place-Based Policy
entries.speaker: Aurel Rochell
entries.abstract: Subsidy competition is a large and persistent feature of state and local governments' economic development policy, yet the benefits of such location incentives remain unclear. I analyze whether subsidy competition can be justified from a place-based policy perspective. I first identify the geolocations of Million Dollar Plant openings to show that subsidy competition does not prevent manufacturing firms from sorting into ex-ante less distressed neighborhoods. Combining these locations with block-level employer-employee matched job counts in a spatial difference-in-differences design, I find that job creation and job take-up are concentrated near opened plants, making take-up regressive over neighborhood incomes due to positive firm sorting. Job-to-job flows indicate that most induced hires are local residents but rarely come from non-employment, implying only moderate reductions in local unemployment. Overall, location incentives generate employment at high cost and predominantly in high-income neighborhoods, implying meaningful welfare costs under redistributive motives and limited viability as place-based policy.

entries.seminar_title: The urban transportation problem: Accessibility in 1100 cities and 400,000 neighborhoods
entries.speaker: Gilles Duranton
entries.abstract: Cities exist to facilitate residents’ access to each other, including to jobs and to a variety of local  services. Differences in accessibility across cities remain poorly measured, especially in low-  and middle-income countries, where most future urban growth will take place. We develop  a new methodology to measure accessibility with a price index, and apply it to over 400,000  neighborhoods of 1,105 cities in 111 countries. Our accessibility index can be decomposed into  a speed index (fast travel) and a distance index (close venues). Accessibility by private vehicle  varies widely across cities, mostly because of differences in distance rather than speed. Cities  where residents live close to venues tend to have slower driving speeds, but not slower transit  speeds. This speed-distance trade-off for private vehicles can be almost entirely accounted for  by two overlapping factors: (1) overall city density (of people and venues), irrespective of their  location within the city, and (2) the coagglomeration of people and venues within cities.

entries.seminar_title: Bases and the City: Spatial Economics of US Military Bases in Okinawa
entries.speaker: Atsushi Yamagishi (山岸 敦)
entries.abstract: Rising geopolitical tensions underscore the strategic importance of military bases and the consumption demand and employment they generate are central to policy debates about their economic benefits for host communities. We assess their spatial economic impacts using newly digitized data from postwar Okinawa, a region heavily exposed to US bases. We document substantial urbanization around US bases, with service-sector expansion but little manufacturing growth. We develop a quantitative spatial model calibrated to Okinawa in 1970 to quantify the role of base-sourced consumption demand and employment. Removing these channels reduces population in base-exposed municipalities and shifts activity from services toward agriculture and manufacturing. Okinawa-wide welfare falls by 7.25% and GNI by 11.99%, although these channels accounted for roughly 30% of GNI. Sectoral reallocation mitigates these losses alongside sizable migration. Suggestive evidence also points to an additional role for past investment in infrastructure and durable capital around US bases.
